# Local resolution weighted composite of Martigny

This tutorial runs the whole pipeline, from search to composites, for an area
around Martigny in the Swiss canton of Valais. The town is surrounded by
mountains, whose steep slopes are challenging terrain for SAR. The tutorial
compares a composite of the ascending orbits, one of the descending orbits,
and one that combines both with local resolution weighting (LRW).

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path

from dotenv import load_dotenv

root = next(p for p in (Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents) if (p / "pyproject.toml").exists())
load_dotenv(root / ".env")
(root / "cache/docs").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
os.chdir(root / "cache/docs")
```

## Find the grid square and its bursts

The area lies in one 10 km square of the MGRS grid. The search covers the
square whole, as in
[From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd#find-the-bursts-of-every-square),
and keeps the VV bursts of August 2025 that reach it:

```{python}
from shapely.geometry import box
from s1bursts import (
    BurstCatalog, BurstProcessor, FileManager, MGRSGrid, ResolutionWeighter,
    RTCConfig, SearchQuery, TimeRange,
)

fm = FileManager("data/martigny")
catalog = BurstCatalog(fm)
aoi = box(7.01, 46.09, 7.055, 46.125)
window = TimeRange("2025-08-01", "2025-08-31")
(square,) = MGRSGrid(aoi, resolution=20)  # the area lies in one square
print(square.mgrs_code, square.crs)

search_area = box(*square.geographic_extent.boundingbox)
found = catalog.search(SearchQuery(time_range=window, intersects=search_area, polarization="VV"))
bursts = found.intersecting(square)

bursts.df.groupby(["pass_direction", "rel_orbit_number"]).agg(
    acquisitions=("date", lambda dates: dates.dt.date.nunique()),
    bursts=("burst_id", "size"),
    sub_swaths=("sub_swath", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.unique()))),
    satellites=("parent_product_name", lambda names: ", ".join(sorted(names.str[:3].unique()))),
)
```

One ascending and two descending orbits cover the square, each imaged five
times in August, with 35 bursts in total.

## Process the bursts

The bursts are processed in the UTM zone of the square, at the 20 m pixel size
of the composites:

```{python}
#| output: false
catalog.download(bursts).raise_on_failure()
processor = BurstProcessor(fm)
rtc = processor.create_backscatter(
    bursts, crs=square.crs, config=RTCConfig(grid_spacing=20),
).raise_on_failure().products
```

## Compose the square

`compose_rtc_by_pass()` composes the square once per pass direction, and
`compose_rtc_lrw()` composes it across both directions and also writes the quality layers. For an area of
several squares,
[From an area to composites](area-to-composites.qmd#compose-each-square) loops
over them.

```{python}
weighter = ResolutionWeighter(fm)
lrw = weighter.compose_rtc_lrw(rtc, square, write_qa=True, time_range=window)
by_pass = weighter.compose_rtc_by_pass(rtc, square, time_range=window)
```

## Compare the viewing directions

Sentinel-1 looks to the right of its track: east on ascending passes, west on
descending ones. Each direction therefore resolves different slopes finely
([Why mountains need it](resolution-weighting.qmd#why-mountains-need-it)), and
a slope in its radar shadow has no value in that direction.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Backscatter composites of August 2025 in a 4 by 4 km window west of Martigny: the five ascending acquisitions (left), the ten descending acquisitions (middle), and all fifteen combined with LRW (right). White marks radar shadow, where a composite has no value."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from s1bursts.product import Layer


def read(composite, layer=Layer.MEASUREMENT):
    """Read one layer of a composite, with its extent in kilometers for imshow."""
    with fm.open(composite, layer) as src:
        left, bottom, right, top = (v / 1000 for v in src.bounds)
        return src.read(1).astype("float32"), [left, right, bottom, top]


view = (346, 350, 5106, 5110)  # easting and northing in km, UTM zone 32N
composites = {
    "Ascending": read(by_pass["Ascending"]),
    "Descending": read(by_pass["Descending"]),
    "LRW": read(lrw),
}
viridis = plt.get_cmap("viridis").copy()
viridis.set_bad("white")  # pixels without a value: radar shadow

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 3.2), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, (name, (data, extent)) in zip(axes, composites.items()):
    image = ax.imshow(10 * np.log10(data), extent=extent, cmap=viridis, vmin=-15, vmax=0)
    ax.set(title=name, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=view[:2], ylim=view[2:])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes, shrink=0.8, label="Gamma-0 (dB)")
plt.show()
```

Each pass composite has gaps on the steep slopes facing away from its
direction, and smears the slopes facing it into coarse streaks. The LRW
composite has a value everywhere in this window, and on each slope it leans toward the
direction that sees the slope finely.

## Read the quality layers

The LRW composite comes with two quality layers, shown here for the same
window:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The LRW composite (left), the number of observations (middle), and the composite quality map in decibels (right). The lightest pixels of the quality map are the most coarsely resolved, not missing."
layers = {
    "LRW composite (dB)": (Layer.MEASUREMENT, dict(cmap="viridis", vmin=-15, vmax=0)),
    "Number of observations": (Layer.QA_NUM, dict(cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=15)),
    "Composite quality map (dB)": (Layer.QA_CQM, dict(cmap="Blues", vmin=-16, vmax=8)),
}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.6, 3.8), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, (title, (layer, style)) in zip(axes, layers.items()):
    data, extent = read(lrw, layer)
    if layer != Layer.QA_NUM:
        data = 10 * np.log10(data)
    fig.colorbar(ax.imshow(data, extent=extent, **style), ax=ax, orientation="horizontal")
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Easting (km)", xlim=view[:2], ylim=view[2:])
axes[0].set_ylabel("Northing (km)")
plt.show()
```

The number of observations (`QA-NUM`) counts the acquisitions that contribute
to each pixel: all fifteen almost everywhere, fewer where one direction sees
only radar shadow. The composite quality map (`QA-CQM`) rates the combined
resolution of each pixel. It is highest on slopes facing away from some orbits
and lowest on the steepest slopes, which every orbit sees squeezed or
not at all. A pixel with a low quality describes the ground more coarsely than
its 20 m pixel size suggests.
[Local resolution weighting](resolution-weighting.qmd) explains both layers.
